variants.title: Trace the training loop
variants.context: A training run moves through four stages: snapshot the inputs under one run identifier, train and checkpoint complete state, evaluate the protected validation data, then gate or investigate. The model changes only after the data path, the optimization path, and the evaluation path have all reported.
variants.prompt: A team starts a new run for a churn model with a fresh dataset version. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Run validation on the protected split at a fixed cadence and retain per-slice metrics.
Materialize the dataset manifest, split rule, feature code, configuration, and baseline checkpoint under one run identifier.
Compare the candidate with the declared baseline and promote only an explainable improvement.
Load batches, compute loss, update parameters, and checkpoint complete state at the recovery interval.

variants.hint: Which stage makes the run reproducible later?
variants.explanation: A run is a controlled experiment: freeze inputs first, then learn, then measure on protected data, then decide.

variants.title: Trace the training loop
variants.context: A training run moves through four stages: snapshot the inputs under one run identifier, train and checkpoint complete state, evaluate the protected validation data, then gate or investigate. The model changes only after the data path, the optimization path, and the evaluation path have all reported.
variants.prompt: Validation loss is far below training loss from the first epoch, and an engineer suspects a leaked feature. Put the stages of that run in order, ending with the decision.

items.text: Training produced falling loss and checkpoints that included optimizer and data position.
The gate stops the run for a data contract failure and sends the split and features back for audit.
The run recorded its dataset version, split rule, label cutoff, and feature code under one identifier.
Validation on the protected split returned results that are implausibly better than training.

variants.hint: An implausible validation result is an evaluation event, not a promotion event.
variants.explanation: Stop invalid evaluations before they consume the budget, because a leaked feature makes every later comparison meaningless.

variants.title: Trace the training loop
variants.context: A training run moves through four stages: snapshot the inputs under one run identifier, train and checkpoint complete state, evaluate the protected validation data, then gate or investigate. The model changes only after the data path, the optimization path, and the evaluation path have all reported.
variants.prompt: A run is moving from one device to eight data-parallel workers. Put the stages in order, keeping the snapshot honest about the new run shape.

items.text: Evaluate the protected split with the same split rule the single-device baseline used.
Snapshot the manifest, configuration, seeds, and the shard assignment each worker will read.
Compare throughput, peak memory, and validation quality with the recorded single-device baseline before keeping the change.
Train with synchronized gradients and checkpoint model, optimizer, scheduler, random state, and data cursor.

variants.hint: What has to be identical for the distributed result to be comparable?
variants.explanation: Scale-out is only evidence when the split rule and baseline stay fixed, so the comparison measures the change and not a new evaluation.

variants.title: Run the incident loop
variants.context: When a run misbehaves, the operating loop is observe, contain, reproduce, then release or roll back. Containment protects the failing evidence and prevents accidental promotion before anyone diagnoses the cause.
variants.prompt: Loss becomes NaN at step 40000 of a mixed-precision run. Put the operating steps in order.

items.text: Stop the run, retain the failing checkpoint and the input interval, and block promotion of its artifacts.
Join metrics, logs, configuration, data manifest, and hardware allocation under the same run identifier.
Roll back to the last accepted checkpoint or release a repaired run through the reversible path.
Replay a bounded control on the same inputs to separate a numerical issue from a transient device fault.

variants.hint: What has to be preserved before anything is restarted?
variants.explanation: Containment comes before diagnosis, because a restarted run destroys the evidence that names the cause.

variants.title: Run the incident loop
variants.context: When a run misbehaves, the operating loop is observe, contain, reproduce, then release or roll back. Containment protects the failing evidence and prevents accidental promotion before anyone diagnoses the cause.
variants.prompt: The overall validation metric is green, but one protected cohort misses its gate. Put the response in order.

items.text: Rerun the cohort evaluation on the same checkpoint to confirm the regression is real and not an evaluation fault.
Hold the candidate artifact immutable and mark it as not promotable while the cohort is investigated.
Read the per-slice metrics next to the run configuration and the data manifest that produced them.
Escalate the quality regression and keep the previous model serving until the cohort gate passes.

variants.hint: A green average is not a passing gate.
variants.explanation: Escalate when any protected cohort misses its gate, because a global average hides the failure the gate exists to catch.

variants.title: Run the incident loop
variants.context: When a run misbehaves, the operating loop is observe, contain, reproduce, then release or roll back. Containment protects the failing evidence and prevents accidental promotion before anyone diagnoses the cause.
variants.prompt: A worker disappears from an eight-way run after a node failure. Put the recovery in order.

items.text: Resume the same experiment and confirm the learning curve continues instead of restarting from scratch.
Halt the remaining workers so no replica keeps updating from an inconsistent gradient view.
Record the worker loss as an experiment event with the step, shard, and synchronization state at failure.
Reload a compatible checkpoint and verify that the data cursor, scheduler, and random state still match.

variants.hint: Which state has to match before the run counts as the same experiment?
variants.explanation: Only a checkpoint holding model, optimizer, scheduler, random state, and data position resumes the same run rather than starting a new one.

variants.title: Price the accelerator plan
variants.context: The operating budget of a run includes accelerator cost. A planned cost is worker count multiplied by the hourly price of one accelerator multiplied by wall time. Distributed training shortens a large job, but communication and stragglers keep the speedup below linear.
variants.prompt: A vision run is planned on 4 L4 accelerators at 0.80 dollars per accelerator-hour, and the profile estimates 9 hours of wall time. What is the planned accelerator cost?
variants.hint: Every reserved accelerator bills for the whole wall time.
variants.explanation: Planned cost is workers times hourly price times wall time, so the reservation is priced before the hardware is held.

mistakes.feedback: That prices one accelerator for 9 hours and ignores the other three workers.
That prices 4 accelerators for a single hour and drops the 9 hour wall time.

variants.title: Price the accelerator plan
variants.context: The operating budget of a run includes accelerator cost. A planned cost is worker count multiplied by the hourly price of one accelerator multiplied by wall time. Distributed training shortens a large job, but communication and stragglers keep the speedup below linear.
variants.prompt: A text classifier is scheduled on 8 A10 accelerators at 1.35 dollars per accelerator-hour, and the run is expected to take 5 hours. What is the planned accelerator cost?
variants.hint: Count the workers before you count the hours.
variants.explanation: Planned cost is workers times hourly price times wall time, and every worker in a data-parallel group bills for the full run.

mistakes.feedback: That prices a single A10 for 5 hours and ignores the 8 way replication.
That prices 8 A10s for one hour and drops the 5 hour wall time.

variants.title: Price the accelerator plan
variants.context: The operating budget of a run includes accelerator cost. A planned cost is worker count multiplied by the hourly price of one accelerator multiplied by wall time. Distributed training shortens a large job, but communication and stragglers keep the speedup below linear.
variants.prompt: One H100 at 8.50 dollars per accelerator-hour finishes a run in 24 hours. The same run on 4 H100s finishes in 8 hours, not 6, because gradient synchronization is not free. How many more dollars does the distributed plan cost than the single-device plan?
variants.explanation: Distributed training buys wall time, not free compute, and the gap between 8 hours and the ideal 6 hours is what communication costs.

mistakes.feedback: That assumes linear speedup, which would make the two plans cost the same at 6 hours.
That reports the distributed plan's total cost instead of the difference from the single-device plan.

variants.title: Diagnose before you intervene
variants.context: Loss alone does not name a failure. Read the curve shape, the train and validation gap, gradient behavior, and data evidence together, then pick the intervention that treats the leading explanation rather than the one that is easiest to apply.
variants.prompt: Training loss keeps falling, held-out loss starts rising after epoch three, and the late gap is 1.3 loss. Gradient norms stay in their expected band and schema checks are current. What is the leading explanation and fix?
options: Divergence, so lower the learning rate and enable gradient clipping before rerunning.
Leakage, so rebuild the split from entity and time boundaries first.
Overfitting, so regularize and choose a checkpoint from protected validation behavior.
optionFeedback: Divergence shows erratic loss and exploding gradient norms, neither of which appears here.
Leakage makes validation look better than training, not worse, so the split is not the suspect.
Correct, a widening gap with a reversing validation curve is the overfitting signature.
variants.hint: Which curve reverses, and which one keeps improving?
variants.explanation: A rising held-out curve with a widening gap is overfitting, and the fix is a generalization control checked against the protected split.

variants.title: Diagnose before you intervene
variants.context: Loss alone does not name a failure. Read the curve shape, the train and validation gap, gradient behavior, and data evidence together, then pick the intervention that treats the leading explanation rather than the one that is easiest to apply.
variants.prompt: Held-out loss is far below training loss from the very first epoch, and a reviewer notes that one feature may be computed after the label event. What should happen next?
options: Add dropout and a weight penalty, then rerun with the same split rule.
Increase model capacity, since the training curve is the weaker of the two.
Audit the splits and feature definitions, then rebuild them from entity and time boundaries.
optionFeedback: Regularization treats overfitting, and it cannot remove future information from a feature.
More capacity would fit the leaked signal faster and make the invalid result look even better.
Correct, an inverted gap plus a suspect feature is the leakage signature, and the split is what must be repaired.
variants.hint: Which failure makes held-out data look easier than training data?
variants.explanation: Validation that is implausibly good points at leakage, so stop and rebuild the split before any tuning result is trusted.

variants.title: Diagnose before you intervene
variants.context: Loss alone does not name a failure. Read the curve shape, the train and validation gap, gradient behavior, and data evidence together, then pick the intervention that treats the leading explanation rather than the one that is easiest to apply.
variants.prompt: Both curves flatten early and stay flat, gradient updates are near zero across most layers, and annotation disagreement has recently increased. What is the best first move?
options: Stop early and add a weight penalty, because the run has clearly fit the training set.
Cut the learning rate and clip gradients, because the optimizer is unstable.
Check feature coverage and capacity with a small controlled ablation, and review the noisy labels.
optionFeedback: Nothing here shows training-specific fit, so a generalization control has no failure to treat.
Clipping treats exploding norms, and these norms are too small rather than too large.
Correct, a plateau with vanishing updates points at underfitting, and noisy labels are the second contributor to check.
variants.hint: Near-zero updates mean the model is not learning, not that it is learning too much.
variants.explanation: A flat pair of curves with vanishing gradients is underfitting, so add signal or capacity and repair the label noise before changing anything else.

variants.title: Scale for the binding constraint
variants.context: Use a more complex training strategy only after a measured limitation makes the coordination cost worthwhile. Data parallelism answers a wall-time limit, sharding answers a memory limit, federated training answers a data boundary, and continual or active learning answers changing evidence.
variants.prompt: A validated model fits on one accelerator with memory to spare, but the run takes 40 hours and the budget allows 12. What is the first fit?
options: Partition parameters and optimizer state across several accelerators.
Coordinate client updates so the raw records never leave their devices.
Replicate the model across workers, split batches, and synchronize gradients.
optionFeedback: Sharding pays communication cost to solve a memory limit that this run does not have.
Federated training answers a data boundary, and nothing here says the data cannot move.
Correct, wall time is the binding constraint and memory already fits, which is the data-parallel case.
variants.hint: Name the constraint that is actually binding before naming a strategy.
variants.explanation: Data parallelism is the answer to a wall-time limit when one device can already hold the model state.

variants.title: Scale for the binding constraint
variants.context: Use a more complex training strategy only after a measured limitation makes the coordination cost worthwhile. Data parallelism answers a wall-time limit, sharding answers a memory limit, federated training answers a data boundary, and continual or active learning answers changing evidence.
variants.prompt: A larger model no longer fits in accelerator memory even at microbatch one, and the team has four accelerators available. What is the right change?
options: Replicate the model on all four devices and split each batch across them.
Keep one device and raise the batch size to use the accelerator better.
Partition parameters, optimizer state, or activations, and budget for activation transfer.
optionFeedback: Data parallelism replicates the model, so every worker still needs the memory that is already missing.
A larger batch increases memory use, which makes the failure worse rather than better.
Correct, memory is the binding constraint, which is what sharding is for, and transfer cost must be budgeted.
variants.hint: Replication does not shrink the per-device model state.
variants.explanation: When memory is the binding constraint, partition the state and measure communication instead of assuming linear speedup.

variants.title: Scale for the binding constraint
variants.context: Use a more complex training strategy only after a measured limitation makes the coordination cost worthwhile. Data parallelism answers a wall-time limit, sharding answers a memory limit, federated training answers a data boundary, and continual or active learning answers changing evidence.
variants.prompt: A model must keep learning from a task whose data changes every quarter, and stakeholders complain that last quarter's behavior degrades after each refresh. What does the situation call for?
options: Continual learning with retention tests on the previously learned tasks.
Federated learning so client records stay on their own devices.
Model sharding so the checkpoint fits with room for new data.
optionFeedback: Correct, changing evidence with regressions on old tasks is what retention testing and replay address.
Federated training answers a data boundary, and the complaint here is forgetting rather than data locality.
Sharding solves a memory limit, which is not the reported problem.
variants.hint: What evidence is being lost between refreshes?
variants.explanation: A new-task gain is not acceptable when it silently destroys previously useful behavior, so every new checkpoint is tested on retained tasks.
